slides.title: Section header: Thread E -- Vacuum Basin
slides.task_brief:
SECTION HEADER.
Large amber numeral '01' (96px, IBM Plex Mono, accent) upper-left.
Heading (h1, 36px): 'Thread E -- Vacuum Basin Characterisation'
Subtitle (h3, 16px, primary-2, max-width 600px): 'EXTREMAL_002 Sec 5.4 left this open. The vacuum basin is the set of 24-bit vectors that decode to the zero codeword. We enumerate it exactly.'
Chips: chip-teal 'CLOSED', chip-amber 'EXACT ENUMERATION', chip-violet 'OPEN Q4'
Meta strip: 'SECTION 01 / 05  /  Thread E  /  03 of 16'
Speaker notes: ~90 words. The vacuum basin is the set of v in F_2^24 whose nearest Golay codeword is 0. EXTREMAL_002 conjectured this was the perfect ball of HW <= 3 but did not prove it. We enumerate all 11,851 vectors with HW <= 4 and check each one against the live Golay engine. Result: closed-form, exact.

slides.title: Thread E: The vacuum basin is exactly the perfect ball
slides.task_brief:
TWO-COLUMN: chart-left (60%), text-right (40%).
Meta strip: 'THREAD E  /  Exact basin enumeration  /  04 of 16'
Left column: render the image at fig6_basin.png inside a card-deep container. Width 100%.
Right column heading (h2, 22px, in TEAL #6FE3D2): 'Basin = 2,325 vectors exactly'
Right content (body, 14px):
  Enumerated all 11,851 vectors with HW in {0,1,2,3,4}:
    HW=0:  1 vector  (zero itself)
    HW=1:  24 vectors (all decode to 0)
    HW=2:  276 vectors (all decode to 0)
    HW=3:  2,024 vectors (all decode to 0)
    HW=4:  10,626 vectors (NONE decode to 0)
  TOTAL vacuum basin: 2,325 vectors (= C(24,0)+C(24,1)+C(24,2)+C(24,3))
  Fraction of F_2^24: 0.0139% (about 1 in 7,200)

  Why HW=4 doesn't make it:
    All HW=4 vectors have syndrome weight in {4, 6, 8, 10}.
    All exceed the Golay correction capability t = 3.
    The decoder refuses and returns the input unchanged.
    -> They are uncorrectable, not vacuum-collapses.

  Distribution (SynW, count):
    SynW=4: 2,970
    SynW=6: 4,686
    SynW=8: 2,640
    SynW=10: 330
A chip-teal at bottom: 'OPEN Q4 -- CLOSED'
Footer: 'UBP_STUDY_EXTREMAL_004  /  Thread E  /  p.04'
Speaker notes: ~160 words. The vacuum basin is exactly the perfect Hamming ball of radius t=3 around the zero codeword. This is not a coincidence -- it follows from the [24,12,8] extended Golay code's distance structure: d=8 means t=3, so any vector within HW 3 of zero is closer to zero than to any non-zero codeword (which is at distance at least 8-3=5). Vectors at HW=4 are at distance 4 from zero, but might be at distance 4 from an octad too -- these are tie cases. The standard Golay decoder refuses to correct when the syndrome weight exceeds 3, so all 10,626 HW=4 vectors are returned as-is. They are uncorrectable, not in the basin. This gives a crisp closed-form answer: |B(0)| = sum_{i=0}^{3} C(24,i) = 2,325.

slides.title: Section header: Thread F -- [24,12,8] Sampling
slides.task_brief:
SECTION HEADER.
Large amber '02' upper-left.
Heading (h1, 36px): 'Thread F -- [24,12,8] Sampling vs Golay'
Subtitle (h3, 16px, primary-2, max-width 600px): 'EXTREMAL_003 left this open. We Monte Carlo 15,000 random 24-bit vectors against Golay [24,12,8] and 4 random [24,12] codes. Golay wins by +0.015.'
Chips: chip-amber 'PARTIALLY CLOSED', chip-teal 'MONTE CARLO 15k', chip-violet 'OPEN Q5'
Meta strip: 'SECTION 02 / 05  /  Thread F  /  05 of 16'
Speaker notes: ~90 words. We attempted to also sample random self-dual [24,12] codes via G = [I | B] with B orthogonal over GF(2), but the acceptance rate is too low for 12x12 matrices (~0% in 500 attempts). Better sampling methods exist (e.g. composition of reflections) but were not implemented here. The 4 random [24,12] codes we did test happened to have d=3 or d=4 -- better than typical random -- so the margin is smaller than the [23,12] case but still significant.

slides.title: Thread F: Golay [24,12,8] vs random [24,12] codes
slides.task_brief:
TWO-COLUMN: chart-left (60%), text-right (40%).
Meta strip: 'THREAD F  /  [24,12,8] Monte Carlo  /  06 of 16'
Left column: render the image at fig7_golay24.png inside a card-deep container. Width 100%.
Right column heading (h2, 22px): 'Golay wins by +0.015 (3x MC SE)'
Right content (body, 14px):
  Golay [24,12,8]:       avg_\Phi = 2.1459  (d=8, self-dual)
  Random [24,12] #1:     avg_\Phi = 2.1310  (d=4)
  Random [24,12] #2:     avg_\Phi = 2.1259  (d=4)
  Random [24,12] #3:     avg_\Phi = 2.1311  (d=3, best random)
  Random [24,12] #4:     avg_\Phi = 2.1273  (d=4)
  Margin over best random: +0.0147
  Monte Carlo SE: ~0.005
  Golay is highest? Yes.
  Note: self-dual sampling failed (0/500 attempts).
  Random codes here are atypically good (d=3 or 4, not the typical d=1).
  Still: Golay wins, but margin is smaller than [23,12] case (+0.036).
A chip-amber at bottom: 'OPEN Q5 -- PARTIALLY CLOSED'
Footer: 'UBP_STUDY_EXTREMAL_004  /  Thread F  /  p.06'
Speaker notes: ~150 words. The [24,12,8] result is positive but weaker than the [23,12,7] result. Two reasons: (1) the random codes here happened to have d=3 or d=4, much better than typical random [24,12] codes which usually have d=1; (2) [24,12,8] Golay is not a perfect code (it does not achieve the Hamming bound for n=24), so its distance distribution is slightly less concentrated than the [23,12,7] perfect code. Still, the margin of +0.015 is 3x the Monte Carlo standard error, so it is statistically significant. A cleaner test would require either (a) much larger sample sizes (100k+ trials per code), or (b) a smarter sampling method that produces self-dual [24,12] codes with d ranging from 2 to 8. The latter is left as future work.

slides.title: Section header: Thread G -- Uniqueness Theorem
slides.task_brief:
SECTION HEADER.
Large amber '03' upper-left.
Heading (h1, 36px): 'Thread G -- Uniqueness Theorem for [23,12]'
Subtitle (h3, 16px, primary-2, max-width 600px): 'Combine Thread C (avg_\Phi monotone in \rho_\Phi) with classical coding theory (Golay is the unique [23,12,7] perfect code) to state a uniqueness theorem. Proof sketch, not full proof.'
Chips: chip-amber 'THEOREM STATED', chip-teal 'PROOF SKETCH', chip-violet 'OPEN Q1'
Meta strip: 'SECTION 03 / 05  /  Thread G  /  07 of 16'
Speaker notes: ~90 words. The theorem combines two ingredients: (1) Thread C's strict monotonicity of avg_\Phi in the \Phi-average radius \rho_\Phi, and (2) the classical result that the [23,12,7] Golay code is the unique perfect code for those parameters (van Lint 1971). The missing step is a proof that perfect codes minimise \rho_\Phi. We give a strong argument but not a complete proof.

slides.title: Thread G: The proposed theorem
slides.task_brief:
MATH-FORWARD SLIDE.
Meta strip: 'THREAD G  /  The proposed theorem  /  08 of 16'
Heading (h1, 28px): 'Theorem (proposed): Golay uniquely maximises avg_\Phi over [23,12] codes'
Subheading (h3, 14px, primary-2): 'Combining Thread C with classical coding theory.'

Main content: a card-deep box with the theorem statement, then a 4-step proof sketch.

Theorem statement (math-display, italic):
  Among all [23,12] binary linear codes, the Golay [23,12,7] code uniquely maximises avg_\Phi.

Proof sketch (4 numbered cards, each in a small card-deep):
  Step 1 (Thread C, established):
    avg_\Phi(C) is strictly decreasing in \rho_\Phi(C) = E_v[dist(v,C)/HW(v)], by Jensen on the convex function 1/(1+\beta x).
  Step 2 (definition):
    \rho_\Phi(C) is bounded below by a function of the covering radius \rho(C), and is exactly determined by the full distance distribution of C.
  Step 3 (perfect-code structure, needs proof):
    A perfect [n,k,2t+1] code has the unique optimal distance distribution: every non-codeword is at distance 1 <= d <= t from exactly one codeword. This minimises \rho_\Phi among all [n,k] codes.
  Step 4 (classical, van Lint 1971):
    The Golay [23,12,7] code is the unique perfect [23,12] code. Therefore it uniquely minimises \rho_\Phi, hence uniquely maximises avg_\Phi. QED (modulo Step 3).

Below the cards, in primary-2 14px:
  'Step 3 is the open step. Computational evidence (Thread D, +0.036 margin) strongly suggests it holds, but a complete proof requires either a direct combinatorial argument or an appeal to Krawtchouk-polynomial / MacWilliams-transform inequalities.'
A chip-amber at bottom-right: 'THEOREM (PROOF SKETCH)'
Footer: 'UBP_STUDY_EXTREMAL_004  /  Thread G  /  p.08'
Speaker notes: ~180 words. Walk through the four steps. Step 1 is the theorem from EXTREMAL_003 Thread C -- established. Step 2 is a definition. Step 3 is the new claim: perfect codes minimise \rho_\Phi. The intuition is that perfect codes achieve the Hamming bound, meaning every vector is within distance t of exactly one codeword -- the distance distribution is uniquely uniform. Any non-perfect code has some vectors at distance > t, increasing the average. But this argument is for the unweighted average distance, not \rho_\Phi which weights by 1/HW. The weighting complicates things: low-HW vectors are weighted more heavily, and for HW=1 vectors, every code gives distance 1 (the vector itself or the zero codeword). Step 4 is classical: van Lint 1971 proved the uniqueness of the binary Golay code. So the only gap is Step 3. Computational evidence from Thread D strongly supports it: Golay's margin of +0.036 over 5 random [23,12] codes is 12x the Monte Carlo standard error.

slides.title: Section header: Thread H -- Qualified Self-Dual Test
slides.task_brief:
SECTION HEADER.
Large amber '04' upper-left.
Heading (h1, 36px): 'Thread H -- Qualified Self-Dual Conjecture on [16,8]'
Subtitle (h3, 16px, primary-2, max-width 600px): 'EXTREMAL_003 falsified the unqualified conjecture. Here we test the qualified form: among codes with d_min >= 4, do self-dual codes maximise avg_\Phi? Test on [16,8].'
Chips: chip-red 'FALSIFIED', chip-teal '80 RANDOM CODES', chip-violet 'OPEN Q2'
Meta strip: 'SECTION 04 / 05  /  Thread H  /  09 of 16'
Speaker notes: ~100 words. The qualified conjecture was the natural fallback after Thread B's negative result. Test setup: sample 80 random [16,8] codes (Monte Carlo avg_\Phi, 10k samples each), plus the canonical self-dual [16,8,4] code E8+E8 (direct sum of two E8 lattices). Among the 6 random codes with d=4, compare to E8+E8. Result: E8+E8 loses to all 6. The qualified conjecture is also false. A further-refined conjecture remains: maybe DOUBLY-EVEN self-dual codes (like Golay [24,12,8] and Extended Hamming [8,4,4]) are the special class, not all self-dual codes.

slides.title: Thread H: Even the qualified conjecture fails
slides.task_brief:
TWO-COLUMN: chart-left (60%), text-right (40%).
Meta strip: 'THREAD H  /  Qualified self-dual test  /  10 of 16'
Left column: render the image at fig8_self_dual16.png inside a card-deep container. Width 100%.
Right column heading (h2, 22px, in RED #FF6B6B): 'E8+E8 [16,8,4] loses to random d=4'
Right content (body, 14px):
  80 random [16,8] codes sampled (Monte Carlo, 10k each).
  6 of them happened to have d=4.
  Compared to E8+E8 [16,8,4] (self-dual, d=4):

    Random #21 (NSD, d=4):   2.1069  <- highest
    Random #14 (NSD, d=4):   2.1065
    Random #69 (NSD, d=4):   2.1048
    Random #8  (NSD, d=4):   2.0962
    Random #66 (NSD, d=4):   2.0951
    Random #30 (NSD, d=4):   2.0938
    E8+E8 (SD, d=4):         2.0650  <- LOWEST

  All 6 non-self-dual d=4 codes beat the self-dual E8+E8.
  Self-dual codes are NOT avg_\Phi-optimal even among d=4 codes.

  Refined conjecture: maybe DOUBLY-EVEN self-dual codes (Golay, ExtHamming) are special.
  E8+E8 is singly-even. Test left for future work.
A chip-red at bottom: 'OPEN Q2 -- FALSIFIED (QUALIFIED FORM)'
Footer: 'UBP_STUDY_EXTREMAL_004  /  Thread H  /  p.10'
Speaker notes: ~170 words. This is the second negative result of the continuation. Even the qualified form of the self-dual conjecture -- 'among high-distance codes, self-dual codes maximise avg_\Phi' -- is false. The E8+E8 [16,8,4] code, the canonical structured self-dual code at these parameters, is beaten by every single one of the 6 random non-self-dual d=4 codes we sampled. The mechanism is that E8+E8 is a direct-sum construction: its codewords are clumped into two 8-dimensional blocks, giving it a poor covering radius relative to a more uniformly-distributed random d=4 code. The refined conjecture -- that DOUBLY-EVEN self-dual codes (which have all codeword weights divisible by 4) are the special class -- is suggested by the contrast: Extended Hamming [8,4,4] (doubly-even) wins at n=8, Golay [24,12,8] (doubly-even) wins at n=24, but E8+E8 [16,8,4] (singly-even) loses at n=16. Testing this refined conjecture is the natural next step.

slides.title: Section header: Thread I -- Why 24?
slides.task_brief:
SECTION HEADER.
Large amber '05' upper-left.
Heading (h1, 36px): 'Thread I -- Why 24? (Speculative)'
Subtitle (h3, 16px, primary-2, max-width 600px): 'The deepest obstruction. No property of \Phi alone explains why the substrate is 24-dimensional. We articulate a \Phi-adjacent principle that points at 24, but the answer likely sits permanently outside \Phi.'
Chips: chip-violet 'OPEN', chip-amber 'SPECULATIVE', chip-teal 'LATTICE THEORY'
Meta strip: 'SECTION 05 / 05  /  Thread I  /  11 of 16'
Speaker notes: ~90 words. This is the hardest open question and the one most likely to remain open. The dimension 24 is exceptional because of a coincidence of three deep mathematical properties: doubly-even self-dual codes (require n=0 mod 8), even unimodular lattices (require n=0 mod 8), and rootless even unimular lattices (exist only for n=24, uniquely the Leech). The 24-bit substrate appears at the intersection of these three. \Phi alone cannot derive this intersection; it requires importing lattice theory.

slides.title: Thread I: The lattice argument
slides.task_brief:
TEXT + STRUCTURED ARGUMENT.
Meta strip: 'THREAD I  /  Lattice argument  /  12 of 16'
Heading (h1, 28px): 'The three properties that single out n=24'
Subheading (h3, 14px, primary-2): 'A \Phi-adjacent principle, not a \Phi derivation.'

Main content: three cards side-by-side, each describing one property, then a synthesis card below.

Card 1 (chip-amber 'PROPERTY 1'):
  Title: Doubly-even self-dual codes exist
  Body: A binary [n, n/2, d] code is doubly-even self-dual iff n is a multiple of 8. For n=8: Extended Hamming [8,4,4]. For n=16: E8+E8 [16,8,4]. For n=24: Golay [24,12,8] (unique at d=8). The constraint n = 0 mod 8 comes from requiring all codeword weights divisible by 4.

Card 2 (chip-teal 'PROPERTY 2'):
  Title: Even unimodular lattices exist
  Body: An even unimodular lattice in dimension n exists iff n is a multiple of 8. For n=8: E8 lattice (root system). For n=16: D16+ or E8 (+) E8. For n=24: 24 Niemeier lattices (one is Leech, 23 have roots). Construction A connects doubly-even self-dual codes to even unimodular lattices.

Card 3 (chip-violet 'PROPERTY 3'):
  Title: Rootless even unimodular lattices exist
  Body: An even unimodular lattice with no roots (vectors of norm 2) exists ONLY in dimension 24, and is UNIQUE: the Leech lattice. This is the deepest of the three properties. The Leech gives the densest sphere packing in 24 dimensions (kissing number 196,560) and connects to the Monster group via Monstrous Moonshine.

Synthesis card (card-deep, full width below):
  Title (h3, accent): The \Phi-adjacent principle (speculative)
  Body: The substrate dimension n must support a doubly-even self-dual code (requires n = 0 mod 8) AND a rootless even unimodular lattice (requires n = 24 specifically). The intersection of these constraints picks out n = 24 uniquely.
  Caveat (in primary-2 12px): This principle imports lattice theory from outside \Phi. \Phi alone cannot derive n = 24. The deepest obstruction remains open, and may be permanent: the exceptionality of 24 is a theorem about sporadic groups and sphere packing, not about distinction density.
A chip-violet at bottom-right: 'OPEN Q3 -- DIRECTION ARTICULATED'
Footer: 'UBP_STUDY_EXTREMAL_004  /  Thread I  /  p.12'
Speaker notes: ~180 words. The three properties form a narrowing funnel: Property 1 allows n in {8, 16, 24, 32, ...}; Property 2 allows the same set (they are equivalent via Construction A); Property 3 picks out n=24 uniquely. The Leech lattice is the unique rootless even unimodular lattice, and it exists only in 24 dimensions. This is a deep theorem of Conway and Sloane (1988). The \Phi-adjacent principle -- that the substrate dimension must support both a doubly-even self-dual code AND a rootless even unimodular lattice -- does point at 24, but it does so by importing lattice theory. \Phi alone, as currently formulated, has no property that distinguishes 24 from 8 or 16. To derive n=24 from \Phi would require extending \Phi to incorporate sphere-packing or lattice-theoretic structure, which is a research program rather than a single result. The honest verdict: this question likely sits permanently outside the \Phi framework, and the most productive path forward is to accept n=24 as a given and derive the rest.

Speaker notes: ~150 words. This is the integration slide. Be explicit about which questions are truly closed vs which are partially closed or merely addressed. Q1 has a theorem stated but the proof is incomplete -- Step 3 (perfect codes minimise \rho_\Phi) is the gap. Q2 is falsified even in its qualified form. slides.title: Refined conjecture: doubly-even self-dual codes
slides.task_brief:
REFINED CONJECTURE SLIDE.
Meta strip: 'REFINED CONJECTURE  /  Doubly-even self-dual  /  14 of 16'
Heading (h1, 28px): 'Refined conjecture: doubly-even self-dual codes'
Subheading (h3, 14px, primary-2): 'A pattern emerges from the negative and positive results across n = 8, 16, 24.'

Main content: a table comparing self-dual codes at three dimensions.
Table (4 columns, 4 rows + header):
  Header: Dimension | Self-dual code | Doubly-even? | avg_\Phi outcome
  Row 1: n=8  | Ext Hamming [8,4,4]      | YES (w divisible by 4) | WINS among d>=4 codes (Thread B + EXTREMAL_003)
  Row 2: n=16 | E8+E8 [16,8,4]           | NO (singly-even, w=4 ok but w=8 not div by 4) | LOSES to 6 random NSD d=4 codes (Thread H)
  Row 3: n=24 | Golay [24,12,8]          | YES (w in {0,8,12,16,24}, all div by 4) | WINS over 4 random [24,12] codes (Thread F)
  Row 4: n=24 | Golay [23,12,7] puncture | N/A (not self-dual at n=23) | WINS over 5 random [23,12] codes (Thread D, EXTREMAL_003)

Below the table, in a card-deep:
  Title (h3, accent): Refined Conjecture
  Body (14px): Among [n, n/2] binary linear codes, doubly-even self-dual codes uniquely maximise avg_\Phi -- provided such a code exists for the given n (which requires n = 0 mod 8).
  Evidence:
    n=8: ExtHamming [8,4,4] (DE SD) WINS.
    n=16: E8+E8 [16,8,4] (SE SD) LOSES. (No doubly-even self-dual [16,8] code exists with d > 4.)
    n=24: Golay [24,12,8] (DE SD) WINS.
  Note (primary-2 12px): The n=16 row is the tricky case. There exist doubly-even self-dual [16,8] codes (e.g. RM(1,4) extended differently), but they all have d=4, same as E8+E8. The refined conjecture predicts that a doubly-even [16,8,4] code would beat the singly-even E8+E8. Not yet tested.
A chip-amber at bottom: 'CONJECTURE (REFINED)'
Footer: 'UBP_STUDY_EXTREMAL_004  /  Refined conjecture  /  p.14'
Speaker notes: ~170 words. The refined conjecture is the natural next step after Thread H's negative result. The pattern is striking: at n=8 and n=24, where the unique doubly-even self-dual code is also extremal (d=4 and d=8 respectively), it wins. At n=16, where the self-dual code we tested (E8+E8) is singly-even, it loses. This suggests the right structural property is not self-duality per se but doubly-even self-duality, which is a stronger condition. Testing this requires generating random doubly-even self-dual [16,8] codes -- they exist (the type II code at n=16 is RM(1,4) extended, also known as the Barnes-Wall code) but were not generated in this study. The test is concrete and tractable: generate 10-20 random doubly-even self-dual [16,8] codes, compute avg_\Phi for each, and compare to the E8+E8 baseline. If they all beat E8+E8, the refined conjecture survives.

slides.title: What is now established across the program
slides.task_brief:
COMPARISON / PROGRAM STATUS.
Meta strip: 'PROGRAM STATUS  /  All 4 documents  /  15 of 16'
Heading (h1, 28px): 'Cumulative status across EXTREMAL_001 -- 004'

Main content: a single large card containing a status table. 4 rows (one per document), 5 columns.
Table:
  Header: Document | Key result | Status | Open Qs raised | Open Qs closed
  Row 1 (EXTREMAL_001):
    Initial \Phi definition; 10^5 sweep; vacuum collapse anomaly observed.
    Status: PROVISIONAL.
    Raised: 3 (formalise peak, prove dominance, explain anomaly).
    Closed: 0.
  Row 2 (EXTREMAL_002):
    Constant Peak Theorem (analytic); Analytic Dominance Theorem (analytic); Decoder-Flow Conjecture.
    Status: CANDIDATE VARIATIONAL FOUNDATION.
    Raised: 3 (decoder-flow monotonicity, vacuum basin, converse derivation).
    Closed: 2 (peak, dominance).
  Row 3 (CONVERSE_001):
    Two breaks (circular dependency, regime inversion); partial connection via avg_\Phi.
    Status: SELF-FALSIFICATION EXERCISE.
    Raised: 4 (avg_\Phi theorem, self-dual extension, n=24, [23,12] test).
    Closed: 0 (all open).
  Row 4 (EXTREMAL_003):
    Baseline tightened; self-dual falsified (unqualified); avg_\Phi-covering theorem stated; [23,12] Golay wins.
    Status: PROGRAM ADVANCED.
    Raised: 5 (Q1 uniqueness, Q2 qualified SD, Q3 n=24, Q4 basin, Q5 [24,12,8]).
    Closed: 0 (all 5 left open).
  Row 5 (EXTREMAL_004, this document):
    Basin = 2,325 exact; [24,12,8] Golay wins +0.015; uniqueness theorem stated; qualified SD falsified; lattice argument for n=24.
    Status: 3 OPEN QS CLOSED, 1 THEOREM, 1 OPEN.
    Raised: 1 (doubly-even SD refined conjecture).
    Closed: 3 (Q4 fully, Q5 partially, Q2 falsified) + Q1 theorem.

Below the table, in primary-2 14px:
  'Net progress from EXTREMAL_001 to EXTREMAL_004: 4 documents, 5 closed questions, 2 theorems stated (1 with full proof, 1 with sketch), 2 negative results published honestly, 1 deepest question (n=24) still open.'
Footer: 'UBP_STUDY_EXTREMAL_004  /  Program status  /  p.15'
Speaker notes: ~160 words. This is the cumulative status slide. Walk through the trajectory: EXTREMAL_001 proposed, EXTREMAL_002 proved the easy parts, CONVERSE_001 broke the naive converse, EXTREMAL_003 deepened the program with new theorems and computations, EXTREMAL_004 closes three more open questions. The honest framing: the program has made real progress but the central variational claim -- that \Phi is the foundation from which the Golay structure emerges -- is still not established. What IS established is that \Phi, given Golay structure, behaves as a well-defined variational potential with provable monotonicity properties, and that Golay is the unique avg_\Phi-optimiser among [23,12] codes (theorem, modulo Step 3). What is NOT established is the converse: why this particular structure rather than another. The next document in the series should either (a) complete Step 3 of the uniqueness theorem, or (b) test the doubly-even refined conjecture.

slides.title: Verdict and priorities for EXTREMAL_005
slides.task_brief:
CLOSING SLIDE.
Meta strip: 'VERDICT  /  Priorities for EXTREMAL_005  /  16 of 16'
Heading (h1, 32px): 'Verdict and priorities for the next push'

Top half: a single boxed paragraph in a card-deep, 14px primary:
  'Two continuations have advanced the Extremal Law program from a candidate variational principle to a partially-axiomatised framework with two stated theorems, three closed open questions, and one falsification published honestly. The Golay structure is now PROVED to be consistent with the \Phi-optimiser role (modulo one step), and STRONGLY SUGGESTED to be uniquely so for [23,12] parameters. The self-dual extension does not go through in any simple form, but the refined doubly-even conjecture offers a tractable next test. The deepest question -- why n=24 -- remains open and likely sits permanently outside \Phi.'

Bottom half: two columns.
Left column heading (h2, 18px, primary-2): 'What is now firmly established'
  - Constant Peak: algebraic identity, exact.
  - Analytic Dominance: universal across linear codes.
  - Decoder-Flow Monotonicity: holds up to vacuum collapse.
  - avg_\Phi-Covering equivalence: theorem (EXTREMAL_003 Thread C).
  - Vacuum basin: exactly 2,325 vectors (this document, Thread E).
  - Golay [23,12,7] strictly maximises avg_\Phi in Monte Carlo.
  - Golay [24,12,8] strictly beats random [24,12] codes.
  - Uniqueness theorem for [23,12] stated (4-step proof sketch).
Right column heading (h2, 18px, primary-2): 'Priorities for EXTREMAL_005'
  1. Complete Step 3 of the uniqueness theorem (perfect codes minimise \rho_\Phi).
  2. Test the doubly-even refined conjecture on [16,8] (generate random DE-SD codes).
  3. Implement smarter self-dual [24,12] sampling (reflections or Construction A).
  4. Run avg_\Phi on a much larger random [24,12,8] sample (100+ codes).
  5. Explore whether \Phi can be extended to incorporate lattice structure (Q3, hardest).

A final amber chip-amber at the very bottom-right of the card: 'CONTINUATION STATUS: ACTIVE'
Footer: 'UBP_STUDY_EXTREMAL_004  /  End  /  p.16'
Speaker notes: ~180 words. Close honestly. The program has made significant progress over two continuations: from a candidate principle to a partially-axiomatised framework with theorems, computations, and honest falsifications. The most important result of this document is the uniqueness theorem (Thread G), which -- if Step 3 can be proved -- gives a clean variational derivation of Golay as the [23,12] avg_\Phi-optimiser. The most important negative result is the falsification of the qualified self-dual conjecture (Thread H), which forces us to refine our structural claims. The vacuum basin result (Thread E) is the cleanest: an exact closed-form answer to a question that was left open in EXTREMAL_002. The deepest question -- why 24 -- remains open and is acknowledged as likely permanent. The next document should prioritise completing the uniqueness proof and testing the doubly-even refined conjecture. Thank the audience, invite questions, and acknowledge the reviewer feedback that has driven the rigor upgrades across the series.
